label: 24-hour, 2-year storm, change
description: Change in rain in the 24-hour, 2-year storm: an ordinary heavy-rain day, about every other year
details: NOAA Atlas 14 (model’s 1979–2005) → 2050–2079 · mean of GFDL-CM3 and NCAR-CCSM4 · RCP 8.5
method: Percent change in the 24-hour, 2-year storm: 100 × (2050–2079 depth ÷ NOAA Atlas 14 depth − 1). The 2050–2079 depth is the mean of SNAP's DOT precipitation-frequency projections for GFDL-CM3 and NCAR-CCSM4 (WRF-downscaled, RCP 8.5; local netCDFs pcpt_<model>_sum_wrf_24h_2050-2079.nc, interval 2), ~480 m cells averaged to the 1 km grid. Atlas 14 is Volume 7 (Alaska), annual maximum series (hdsc.nws.noaa.gov/pub/hdsc/data/ak/ak2yr24ha_ams.zip, 1/1000 inch, NAD83 lon/lat), averaged over 3 × 3 points per 1 km cell. SNAP's DOT depths are Atlas 14 × each model's change since 1979–2005 (Bieniek et al. 2022; SNAP's pipeline uses the annual maximum series), so this is the models' projected change since 1979–2005.
pros: Both models project an increase almost everywhere (99 % of land)
An ordinary heavy-rain day: the wear roads and slopes see every other year
cons: The two models don't agree on where the change is largest (rank correlation near 0); the average's pattern mostly follows GFDL-CM3, which projects about twice the change of NCAR-CCSM4
Not the storm that washes out roads; DOT design storms are rarer (25–100 years)
Low agreement with the 100-year change (same class on 41 % of land)
sources: SNAP DOT precipitation frequency, local netCDFs (24h, 2050–2079, interval 2, both models)
author: Joshdpaul
retired: 2026-11-09 (Joshdpaul): team kept the 100-year storm only. Letter F given to another variant (never chosen as a team decision).
